newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia launches modified SS-25 from new cosmodrome.
newsitem.headline: Russia launches modified SS-25 from new cosmodrome.

text.p: Russia staged the first launch from its new Svobodny cosmodrome in the Far East on Tuesday, sending a secret military satellite into orbit aboard a modified SS-25 ballistic missile.

The Start-1 booster rocket blasted off at 0200 GMT from the cosmodrome, which is still under construction at a snowbound former strategic nuclear missile base in Siberia about 9,000 km (6,000 miles) east of Moscow.
Local authorities and environmentalists had protested at plans to jettison parts of booster rockets over the thinly populated region. But the authorities did not delay the launch.
"This satellite will be used for military purposes," a defence ministry official told reporters after the launch of the 87-kg (191 lb) satellite, known as Zeya. He did not elaborate.
The Start-1 is a based on the SS-25 Topol (Poplar) missile originally designed to carry nuclear payloads to North America.

The new cosmodrome, only 100 km (60 miles) from the Chinese border, was developed on orders from President Boris Yeltsin to to reduce dependence on the main Soviet launch site at Baikonur, which Moscow now has to rent from independent Kazakhstan.
Baikonur's maintenance and rent -- $115 million a year -- are the source of endless squabbles between Moscow and Almaty.
"Russia cannot be dependent on Baikonur forever and pay rent to Kazakhstan," said Pyotr Lebedev, deputy commander of Svobodny, which means "Free" in Russian.

The base should eventually become Russia's main launch site due to its good position on the same latitude as Baikonur, although there are no immediate plans to transfer launches of manned space flights from Baikonur.
Svobodny is certainly destined to be the main launch pad for the commercial satellites Moscow is banking on to fund its financially troubled space industry.

Alexander Sukhodolsky, technical director of the Complex-Mit company which produces Start-1 boosters, said that later this year a U.S. satellite would be launched from Svobodny. British and Swedish projects are scheduled to follow.
The space industry, once the pride of the Soviet Union, has fallen on hard times since the superpower collapsed in 1991 and joint ventures with the West are now its main income.
Several flights have been delayed because of cash shortages, while a fire on the ageing manned orbital station Mir last week did little to bolster confidence in Moscow's space programme.
Officials insist that solid-fuel rockets like the Start present no danger to the environment but admit that parts of its boosters do fall to earth after launch.

On Monday protesters, apparently with the backing of the local authorities, reportedly took to the streets of Yakutsk, capital of the diamond-rich ethnic republic of Sakha-Yakutia, north of the new cosmodrome.

Itar-Tass news agency said Yakutia officials had written to the Defence Ministry saying they doubted the safety of the Start rocket and threatening to scrap a 1996 agreement allowing booster components to fall on their territory.
